title: Consumer Protection
summary: Consumer protection means safeguarding consumers against unfair trade practices, defective goods and deficient services, and educating them about their rights and responsibilities. This chapter covers the importance of consumer protection, the Consumer Protection Act 2019 – meaning of consumer, rights and responsibilities, who can file a complaint, the three-tier redressal machinery with its pecuniary limits, and remedies – and the role of consumer organisations and NGOs.

notes.heading: Meaning and Importance of Consumer Protection
notes.html:
Consumer protection means protecting consumers from unfair trade practices (adulteration, overcharging, misleading advertisements, defective goods, deficient services) and educating them about their rights and responsibilities. The maxim has shifted from caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) to caveat venditor (let the seller beware).

Importance from the consumers' point of view:

  1. Consumer ignorance – most consumers are unaware of their rights and remedies.
  2. Unorganised consumers – consumers are scattered and weak compared to sellers.
  3. Widespread exploitation of consumers – through adulteration, short weights, spurious goods, false claims and dark patterns online.

Importance from the business point of view:

  1. Long-term interest of business – satisfied customers bring repeat sales and goodwill.
  2. Business uses society's resources – so it should supply goods in the public interest.
  3. Social responsibility – business has responsibilities towards consumers as a stakeholder.
  4. Moral justification – it is the moral duty of business to avoid exploitation.
  5. Government intervention – if business ignores consumer interests, the government may impose strict controls, harming its image.

notes.heading: Consumer Protection Act, 2019: Meaning of Consumer
notes.html:
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the Act of 1986 and came into force on 20 July 2020 (most provisions). It covers all goods and services (unless exempted) and all modes of transactions – offline and online, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing.

Consumer means any person who:

  • buys goods for a consideration that has been paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment; it includes any user of such goods with the approval of the buyer; or
  • hires or avails services for a consideration; it includes any beneficiary of such services with the approval of the person who hired them.

A person who obtains goods for resale or any commercial purpose is not a consumer. However, goods bought and used exclusively for earning livelihood by self-employment are not treated as commercial purpose (e.g. a tailor buying a sewing machine is a consumer).

Key features of the 2019 Act: establishment of the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA); complaints can be filed where the complainant resides or works; e-filing of complaints (e-Daakhil portal); mediation as an alternative dispute resolution; product liability of manufacturers, sellers and service providers; penalties for misleading advertisements, including on endorsers; protection against unfair contracts.

notes.heading: Rights of Consumers
notes.html:
1. Right to safety – right to be protected against marketing of goods and services that are hazardous to life and property (e.g. substandard electrical appliances).
  2. Right to be informed – right to complete information about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, price, date of manufacture and expiry.
  3. Right to choose – right to be assured access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices.
  4. Right to be heard – right to have one's interests receive due consideration at appropriate forums; to file complaints.
  5. Right to seek redressal – right to get relief against unfair or restrictive trade practices and exploitation (replacement, refund, compensation).
  6. Right to consumer awareness (education) – right to acquire the knowledge and skills to be an informed consumer throughout life.

Memory aid: SICHRE – Safety, Information, Choice, Heard, Redressal, Education.

notes.heading: Responsibilities of Consumers
notes.html:
• Be aware of various goods and services available so as to make a wise choice.
  • Buy only standardised goods as they guarantee quality: ISI mark on electrical goods, FPO mark on food products, Hallmark on gold jewellery, Agmark on agricultural products, ISO certification.
  • Learn about the risks associated with products and follow the manufacturer's instructions.
  • Read labels carefully for information on price, net weight, manufacturing and expiry dates.
  • Assert yourself to ensure you get a fair deal.
  • Be honest in dealings; choose only legal goods and services; avoid black marketing and hoarding.
  • Ask for a cash memo (bill) on purchase – it serves as proof of purchase.
  • File a complaint in an appropriate consumer forum in case of a shortcoming.
  • Form consumer societies to educate consumers.
  • Respect the environment; avoid waste, littering and pollution.

notes.heading: Who Can File a Complaint
notes.html:
1. A consumer to whom goods are sold or services provided (or agreed to be).
  2. Any voluntary consumer association registered under any law in force.
  3. The Central Government or any State Government.
  4. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).
  5. One or more consumers having the same interest, on behalf of numerous consumers (class action).
  6. The legal heir or legal representative of a deceased consumer.
  7. The parent or legal guardian of a consumer who is a minor.
  8. The husband, relative or any person on behalf of a consumer under certain conditions as allowed by the Act.

A complaint must normally be filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose.

notes.heading: Redressal Machinery: Three-tier Consumer Commissions
notes.html:
The Act sets up a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery. The pecuniary jurisdiction is decided on the basis of the value of goods or services paid as consideration.

BasisDistrict CommissionState CommissionNational Commission
LevelEach district, set up by the State GovernmentEach state, set up by the State GovernmentNational level (New Delhi), set up by the Central Government
CompositionPresident and at least two membersPresident and at least four membersPresident and at least four members
Pecuniary limit (as revised by the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021)Up to ₹50 lakhAbove ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 croreAbove ₹2 crore
Limit originally stated in the Act (2019)Up to ₹1 crore₹1 crore to ₹10 croreAbove ₹10 crore
Appeal against its orderTo State Commission within 45 daysTo National Commission within 30 daysTo Supreme Court within 30 days

Pre-deposit for appeal: an appeal against a District Commission order requires deposit of 50% of the amount ordered; similar 50% pre-deposits apply to appeals against State and National Commission orders.

Note for exams: NCERT textbooks state the figures in the original Act (₹1 crore / ₹10 crore). The limits currently in force since 30 December 2021 are ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore. Mention the current limits and, if needed, the original figures.

Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) – a regulator set up by the Central Government to protect, promote and enforce the rights of consumers as a class: it can investigate violations, order recall of unsafe goods, order discontinuation of unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements, and impose penalties.

notes.heading: Remedies (Reliefs) Available to Consumers
notes.html:
If the Commission is satisfied that the complaint is genuine, it may order the opposite party to:

  1. Remove the defect in goods or deficiency in service.
  2. Replace the defective product with a new one free from defect.
  3. Refund the price paid.
  4. Pay compensation for any loss or injury suffered due to negligence.
  5. Pay punitive damages in appropriate circumstances.
  6. Discontinue the unfair or restrictive trade practice and not repeat it.
  7. Not offer hazardous goods for sale.
  8. Withdraw hazardous goods from sale.
  9. Cease manufacture of hazardous goods and desist from offering hazardous services.
  10. Pay a sum determined by the Commission (subject to a minimum percentage of the value of the defective goods or deficient services, as laid down in the Act) into a consumer welfare fund, where loss or injury has been suffered by a large number of consumers who cannot be easily identified.
  11. Issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of a misleading advertisement.
  12. Pay adequate costs to the complainant.

notes.heading: Consumer Awareness: Role of Consumer Organisations and NGOs
notes.html:
Consumer organisations and NGOs work to protect and promote consumer interests (e.g. Consumer Guidance Society of India, Mumbai; Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad; Common Cause, New Delhi; VOICE, Delhi).

  1. Educating the public about consumer rights through training programmes, seminars and workshops.
  2. Publishing periodicals and other publications to spread knowledge about consumer problems, legal remedies and other matters.
  3. Carrying out comparative testing of consumer products in accredited laboratories and publishing results.
  4. Encouraging consumers to protest and take action against exploitative and unfair trade practices.
  5. Providing legal assistance to consumers through aid and legal advice.
  6. Filing complaints in consumer commissions on behalf of consumers.
  7. Taking initiative in filing cases in the interest of the general public (public interest litigation).

Other ways of consumer protection: self-regulation by business; business associations such as FICCI and CII laying down codes of conduct; consumer awareness; government (legal framework such as the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006, Legal Metrology Act 2009, Bureau of Indian Standards Act 2016, Competition Act 2002).

keyTerms.definition: A person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, not for resale or commercial purpose; includes users or beneficiaries with the buyer's approval.
'Let the buyer beware' – the old principle that the buyer must check quality himself.
'Let the seller beware' – the modern principle that the seller is responsible for quality.
The law that replaced the 1986 Act, effective from 20 July 2020, covering online and offline transactions and setting up the CCPA.
Central Consumer Protection Authority – regulator that protects and enforces consumer rights as a class, including recalls and action against misleading advertisements.
Lowest tier of consumer redressal; hears complaints where the value paid for goods or services is up to ₹50 lakh (current limit).
Middle tier; hears complaints above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore, and appeals from District Commissions.
Apex consumer commission; hears complaints above ₹2 crore and appeals from State Commissions.
Damages awarded to punish the opposite party for serious wrongdoing, beyond compensation for actual loss.
An advertisement ordered by a Commission or CCPA to neutralise the effect of an earlier misleading advertisement.
Standardisation mark of the Bureau of Indian Standards, used mainly on electrical and industrial products.
Certification mark of purity on gold and silver jewellery.

mcqs.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (with the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules), a complaint regarding a car bought for ₹35 lakh should be filed with the:
mcqs.explanation: The value paid is up to ₹50 lakh, so the District Commission has jurisdiction.

mcqs.q: Ramesh paid ₹1.2 crore for a flat that has serious construction defects. Where should he file his complaint under the current limits?
mcqs.explanation: Value above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore falls under the State Commission.

mcqs.q: An appeal against the order of the State Commission can be made to the National Commission within:
mcqs.explanation: Appeal from State to National Commission lies within 30 days; from District to State it is 45 days.

mcqs.q: Priya was not told by the seller that a skin cream contained an ingredient she is allergic to. Which right was violated?
mcqs.explanation: Not disclosing ingredients violates the right to be informed.

mcqs.q: A pressure cooker burst due to a manufacturing defect, injuring the user. Which right of the consumer was violated?
mcqs.explanation: Marketing of goods hazardous to life violates the right to safety.

mcqs.q: Which of the following persons is NOT a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act 2019?
options: A student buying a laptop for studies
A tailor buying a sewing machine to earn his livelihood
A trader buying 100 mobile phones for resale
A person using a fan bought by his father
mcqs.explanation: Goods bought for resale are for commercial purpose, so the trader is not a consumer.

mcqs.q: Which mark should a consumer look for while buying gold jewellery?
mcqs.explanation: Hallmark certifies the purity of gold and silver jewellery.

mcqs.q: A company was ordered to publish a new advertisement clarifying that its earlier claim of '100% germ protection' was false. This relief is:
mcqs.explanation: An advertisement to neutralise the effect of a misleading one is a corrective advertisement.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Under the 2019 Act, a consumer can file a complaint where he resides or works.
Reason (R): The 2019 Act aims to make the redressal process more convenient for consumers.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Allowing filing at the place of residence or work (and e-filing) was introduced to make redressal convenient.

mcqs.q: Which body under the 2019 Act can order the recall of unsafe goods and act against misleading advertisements for consumers as a class?
mcqs.explanation: The CCPA protects and enforces the rights of consumers as a class.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Asking for a cash memo is a responsibility of a consumer.
Reason (R): A cash memo serves as proof of purchase while filing a complaint.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: The bill is needed as evidence of purchase, which is why consumers should insist on it.

mcqs.q: A consumer organisation tested five brands of bottled water in a laboratory and published the results. This role is:
options: Carrying out comparative testing of products
Filing complaints on behalf of consumers
mcqs.explanation: Testing products in labs and publishing results is comparative testing.

Who is a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act 2019?
questions.answerHtml: A person who buys goods or hires services for a consideration (paid, promised or deferred), including users or beneficiaries with the buyer's approval, but not one who buys for resale or commercial purpose.

questions.q: Explain the importance of consumer protection from the point of view of business (any three points).
questions.answerHtml:
1. Long-term interest of business – satisfied customers lead to repeat sales, new customers and goodwill.
  2. Business uses society's resources – it is therefore responsible for supplying goods and services in the interest of the public.
  3. Government intervention – if business exploits consumers, the government may impose strict regulations, which damages its public image.

questions.q: State any three responsibilities of a consumer.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Buy standardised goods – look for ISI, FPO, Agmark or Hallmark to ensure quality.
  2. Ask for a cash memo – it serves as proof of purchase.
  3. Read labels carefully – check price, net weight and manufacturing and expiry dates.

questions.q: Who can file a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act 2019? (any four)
questions.answerHtml:
1. A consumer who has bought goods or availed services.
  2. Any registered voluntary consumer association.
  3. The Central Government or any State Government, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority.
  4. One or more consumers with the same interest, on behalf of numerous consumers.
  5. The legal heir or legal representative of a deceased consumer, or the parent or guardian of a minor consumer.

questions.q: Explain the role of consumer organisations and NGOs in protecting and promoting consumer interests (any four points).
questions.answerHtml:
1. Educating the public about consumer rights through training programmes, seminars and workshops.
  2. Publishing periodicals on consumer problems, legal reporting and remedies.
  3. Comparative testing of products in accredited laboratories and publishing the results.
  4. Providing legal assistance and filing complaints in consumer commissions on behalf of consumers, including public interest cases.

questions.q: Explain the three-tier redressal machinery under the Consumer Protection Act 2019.
questions.answerHtml:
1. District Commission

  • Set up by the State Government in each district; consists of a President and at least two members.
  • Hears complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration is up to ₹50 lakh (as revised by the 2021 Rules; the Act originally provided ₹1 crore).
  • Appeal against its order lies with the State Commission within 45 days, on deposit of 50% of the amount ordered.

2. State Commission

  • Set up by the State Government in each state; consists of a President and at least four members.
  • Hears complaints above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore (originally ₹1 crore to ₹10 crore), and appeals from District Commissions.
  • Appeal against its order lies with the National Commission within 30 days.

3. National Commission

  • Set up by the Central Government; consists of a President and at least four members.
  • Hears complaints above ₹2 crore (originally above ₹10 crore), and appeals from State Commissions.
  • Appeal against its order lies with the Supreme Court within 30 days.

questions.q: Nikhil bought an air-conditioner for ₹48,000 from an online platform. It stopped cooling within a week. The seller refused to repair it and ignored his emails. Nikhil kept the invoice and decided to approach a consumer commission. (a) Which right of the consumer is Nikhil exercising? (b) Which responsibility did he fulfil? (c) Where should he file his complaint? (d) State any three reliefs the commission may grant him.
questions.answerHtml:
1. (a) Right to seek redressal (and right to be heard) – the right to get relief against defective goods and unfair practices.
  2. (b) Responsibility of asking for and keeping the bill (cash memo) – it serves as proof of purchase; also the responsibility to file a complaint in case of a shortcoming.
  3. (c) District Commission – the value paid (₹48,000) is within ₹50 lakh. Under the 2019 Act he can file where he resides or works, and online through e-filing, since online purchases are covered.
  4. (d) Reliefs (any three):
    • Remove the defect in the air-conditioner.
    • Replace it with a new defect-free one.
    • Refund the price paid.
    • Pay compensation for the loss or inconvenience suffered, and pay adequate costs.
